title: If not now, when?
hook: Hillel: if I am not for myself, who is for me? if I am only for myself, what am I? if not now, when? (Pirkei Avot 1:14)
tomorrow: strict Shammai had one rule about your face. what was it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simon the Just: the world stands on Torah, worship and kindness, and when the Temple fell, kindness took the weight. Three pillars.

A to-do app usually has a button for later: snooze, someday, remind me tomorrow. Hillel, a sage from the time before the Temple fell, asked the question that button avoids. If I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? Three questions, in Pirkei Avot. The last one sounds like a poster. But the Talmud tells of a very long argument, between Hillel's students and the students of his rival, Shammai, that lands in the same place.
screen: `SNOOZE, SOMEDAY, LATER.` → `IF NOT FOR MYSELF?` → `ONLY FOR MYSELF?` → `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?`

segments.voice: The Talmud says the house of Shammai and the house of Hillel argued for two and a half years over one question: would it have been better for human beings never to have been created? Let both sides speak. The Talmud gives only their answers; the reasons here are how teachers put each side's case. The house of Shammai: better not. A human life carries enormous responsibility, and every day brings the chance to do wrong, to hurt someone, to waste the gift. That's not gloom; it's taking life seriously. The house of Hillel: better to be created. A person is a chance for good that nothing else in the world can be. Then they counted, and the Talmud gives the verdict, which keeps both. It would have been better not to be created. But now that we have been, let a person examine their deeds. That's the turn. The verdict doesn't settle whether life was a good idea in the abstract. It hands the question back as work: you're here, so look at what you do. Hillel's three questions say the same in miniature. Be for yourself; nobody can do your part. Don't be only for yourself. And don't wait. The odd part: the verdict leans toward 'better not,' and it still ends where Hillel's saying does. Now.
screen: `BETTER NEVER TO BE CREATED?` · `SHAMMAI: THE WEIGHT OF A LIFE.` · `HILLEL: A CHANCE FOR GOOD.` · then, large: `NOW, EXAMINE YOUR DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write the one thing you've been snoozing, something for yourself or for someone else, in a few plain words. Under it, write the smallest piece of it you could do today, and the hour you'll do it.
If not now: the end of Hillel's three questions, the one that refuses the snooze button. Im lo achshav in the Hebrew.
Pocket this one: if not now, when, right where both houses ended up. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1473 COUNTS.` → `SAYINGS OF THE FATHERS · 2 OF 6.` → `TOMORROW: STRICT SHAMMAI HAD ONE RULE ABOUT YOUR FACE. WHAT WAS IT?`

howItsDone: Hillel's three questions, from Pirkei Avot, are studied in Jewish homes, schools and synagogues; the Talmud's debate between the houses of Hillel and Shammai is read in Eruvin 13b.

Hillel.meaning: a sage known for patience; his students formed the house of Hillel

Shammai.meaning: a sage known for strictness, Hillel's great rival

Pirkei Avot.meaning: Sayings of the Fathers: a book of rabbinic teachings in the Mishnah

Talmud.meaning: the great collection of rabbinic discussion of Jewish law and lore

sources.ref: Pirkei Avot 1:14 (Hillel: if I am not for myself, who is for me? and if I am only for myself, what am I? and if not now, when?)
